newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel says will honour peace pacts, Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Israel says will honour peace pacts, Mubarak.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman assured Egypt on Monday that the Israeli government would respect and implement agreements it has reached with the Palestinians, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said.
"The president (Weizman) assured me that they are honouring the agreements and it is going to be implemented," Mubarak told a joint news conference with the Israeli head of state.

Weizman, pressed on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's failure to carry out aspects of the agreements, said: "We have had security problems in the past, we hope that we will be over it and we have to be very careful of what we do in the future.

"So therefore the government is not going back. The government perhaps has slowed down but I'm sure, as I've said to President Mubarak, that the government of Israel will continue to do all its best to achieve peace with the Palestinians."
At the news conference he did not go further towards an explicit pledge that Israel would carry out the agreements.

The main issue in dispute is Israel's plan to redeploy its troops in the West Bank town of Hebron. Israel wants to renegotiate arrangements agreed more than one year ago but Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said the agreement must stand.
Mubarak has told Netanyahu he would not meet him unless Israeli troops withdrew from Hebron as stipulated.

Netanyahu's scorn for land-for-peace principles signed with the Palestinians has brought Israel's relations with its neighbours to boiling point, even grating on the nerves of moderate Egypt -- the first Arab country to make peace with the Jewish state and a key regional power.

Weizman, an architect of the 1979 Egyptian-Israeli peace deal and a good friend of assassinated president Anwar Sadat, met Mubarak on a good will mission aimed at convincing an increasingly sceptical Egypt his country was still committed to peace.
His visit, Weizman said, would be to heal ..."certain splits, which everyone sees, with the largest Arab country, and I think we can find a number of directions for improved relations."
Netanyahu's radical policies have galvanised Weizman, whose office is largely ceremonial, into action rare in Israeli presidential history.
An Egyptian government newspaper said on Monday that Netanyahu's government was near collapse.

"Netanyahu is still fumbling around, sticking to the policy of beating about the bush in an attempt to abort the peace agreements, firstly as a political aim of his aggressive strategy and secondly to save his government from collapse," the Al-Akhbar daily said in a front-page editorial.

"Nobody expects to believe Netanyahu when he claims every day there are signs of a solution to the crisis over negotiations with the Palestinians, while the hardline crows in his government...wait in ambush for any move in that direction," the newspaper added.

"The Israeli government is in reality fragmented and at risk of collapse at any moment because of discord and conflicts of interest. (All this) calls for pessimism that Netanyahu is capable of taking a decision in favour of the peace process."
